title: Unravelling drivers of distribution and niche shifts in Antarctic krill through ontogenetic information and model transferability
content:
Abstract
Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) is a keystone species in the Southern Ocean, and shifts in its distribution profoundly influence the structure and functioning of the ecosystem. While species distribution models (SDMs) are widely employed to study such changes, most overlook life-stage-specific responses and the influence of other ecological and physical processes, leading to unreliable estimates of species distributions. To address these limitations, we developed stage-structured SDMs and applied model-transferability analyses (projecting models across distinct time periods to isolate the effects of environmental covariates from non-environmental drivers) to explore spatial distribution dynamics and the mechanisms underlying niche and habitat shifts in krill. The results showed distinct niche differences between the various stages of krill. Specifically, larvae experienced a southward contraction of suitable habitat, along with a narrowing of their niche breadth, whereas juvenile and adult habitats both expanded, shifting northward and southward, respectively. Transferability analysis further indicated that non-environmental drivers (e.g. reproductive relocation, physical advection, and biotic interactions) often outweighed pure environmental tracking in driving these profound spatial decouplings. This stark divergence highlights a clear violation of strict niche conservatism, demonstrating that krill realized niches are highly dynamic across different life stages. By highlighting how ontogenetic stages respond divergently to changing oceans, this study improves our mechanistic understanding of krill redistributions, helping support spatially dynamic and stage-resolved management strategies.
